hint.title: Split test
hint.text: Two checks. 'respectively' is a small add-on, so a comma sets it off. Then: can 'the achievement is known as winning the EGOT' stand alone? If so, sentence one needs STOP punctuation.

hint.title: Who did it?
hint.text: 'Recordings of electrical activity in the brain' is a description. Which noun in the choices IS a recording of brain activity? It must come right after the comma.

hint.title: Point test
hint.text: Whose young? Point at the owner: 'the animal' (one). Then the swap test: 'it is young'?

hint.title: Split test
hint.text: Is 'In modern plays, actors typically won't acknowledge the audience' complete? Does 'To do so breaks the fourth wall…' stand alone too?

hint.title: Who did it?
hint.text: What was 'supported by biochemical analyses'? Vegetables? Diets? Or something from the study? Put that right after the comma.

hint.title: Namely test
hint.text: The first part is a complete sentence. What follows just names the two varieties (it's not a sentence). Can you say 'namely' there?

hint.title: Point test
hint.text: In whose place? The thing that's 'gone': 'the types of pop culture references' (many). Owns, or 'they are'?

hint.title: Who did it?
hint.text: 'Compared to that of alumina glass'—'that' means 'the arrangement'. So an arrangement is being compared. Which choice starts with one?

hint.title: Verb count
hint.text: Find the main verb: '…shows not only…'. The sentence already has it, so the blank only describes the analysis.

hint.title: Own-word test
hint.text: Until recently Theia was ____, but now people claim to have found real pieces of it. Before the evidence, it was only an idea. Which word means that?

hint.title: Take-out test
hint.text: Remove '____ some biologists believe can be used to explain…'. Do you still know which framework? Split test: can 'some biologists believe can be used to explain…' stand alone? Believe WHAT?

hint.title: Point test
hint.text: What becomes susceptible to OBI? Point at it: 'a given term' (one). Ignore the examples between the dashes.

hint.title: Verb count
hint.text: The sentence already has its verbs ('re-created and then reprogrammed'). The blank says WHY they did it. Which form means 'in order to'?

hint.title: Who did it?
hint.text: Who recovered two years later? A person or a reign? That person goes right after the comma.

hint.title: Split test
hint.text: Put a period after 'Tribe'. Is the first part a full sentence? Can 'today, nearly a century later, it is the oldest…' stand alone too?

hint.title: But/and/so test
hint.text: Thomas's story is set inside a big historical event. Then Beulah's story is set inside another big historical event. Same move twice—which bucket?

hint.title: Flip test
hint.text: Flip it: 'the chorus-to-verse ratios of rock and of rap'. Each genre is one thing and owns ratios. Check the apostrophe grid: one owner + owns the next word.

hint.title: Split test
hint.text: Read the part before the blank: 'With a blend of … windows'. Is that a full sentence, or just an opening piece? Piece + sentence is the GO light.

hint.title: Flip test
hint.text: How many variables? (five). Do the variables own anything? Then flip the next part: 'the movement of objects'—objects in general, so how many owners?

hint.title: Take-out test
hint.text: Take the names out: 'in fellow OECD nations, respectively.' Which nations? The names are needed, so nothing separates them from 'nations'.

hint.title: Point test
hint.text: Whose eight panels? Point at the owner: the poems (more than one). Owns, or 'they are'?

hint.title: Verb count
hint.text: The main verb 'assembles' comes later, so the blank can't be a second main verb. And there's a comma after 'environment'—what opens that pair?

hint.title: But/and/so test
hint.text: Sentence 1: the book has vivid prose. Sentence 2: it also has great images. Swap in 'and' or 'but'—which fits? Then pick from that bucket.

hint.title: Who did it?
hint.text: What is 'cheap, versatile, and easy to produce'? That thing must come right after the comma. Watch out for 'there are' and for 's / s' words.

hint.title: Take-out test
hint.text: Take 'however' out: 'Scott-Heron himself resisted the godfather nickname, feeling that…'. Still works, so 'however' is extra. Extra words in the middle get a matching pair.

hint.title: Cover the middle
hint.text: Cover 'the organism uses to protect itself from predation'. What's left: 'the toxins … actually ____'. Toxins = it or they?

hint.title: Who did it?
hint.text: Who is doing the 'assessing' of Kurosawa's films? A person. That person must come right after the comma.

hint.title: Split test
hint.text: Stop after 'tombs': is that a complete sentence? Then does 'these burial chambers seem to blend…' have its own subject and verb?

hint.title: Who did it?
hint.text: Which ice is 'defined by a disorganized molecular structure'? Reread the sentence before. That ice goes right after the comma.

hint.title: Namely test
hint.text: Try saying 'namely' at the blank. Does the second part show HOW the painting uses the whole light spectrum? The first part is already a full sentence.

hint.title: Verb count
hint.text: Main verb: 'honors'. The part between 'Udé' and 'honors' is extra description, closed by a comma after 'excellence'. What opens it, and can an add-on have a main verb?

hint.title: Take-out test
hint.text: Remove 'in the process': '…alter the particles and dismantle any information…'. Still fine? Then 'in the process' is extra and needs a matching pair around it.

hint.title: But/and/so test
hint.text: Sentence 1: the field is split into two camps. Sentence 2: explains who the two camps are. A new point, a contrast, or the same idea said more clearly?

hint.title: List test
hint.text: Count Hayden's responsibilities. The items already contain commas ('collections, which boast…'), and there's a semicolon later. What separates items in a list like that?

hint.title: Verb count
hint.text: Find the real main verb: 'scientists … adapted the test'. The blank sits inside a description of the scientists, so it can't be a second main verb.

hint.title: Split test
hint.text: Can 'among them … Teju Cole, who has written…' stand alone? It has no main verb of its own. Sentence + piece = GO.

hint.title: Goal checklist
hint.text: Goal: why the 1990 discovery matters for PLOT's reputation (being first). The right choice says what was found and what it means for Plot being first. Watch for overstatements like 'disproved'.

hint.title: Split test
hint.text: Find each half's main verb: 'entered' and 'set'. Two subjects, two main verbs → two sentences. The 'Having left…' piece describes the ship in the second one.

hint.title: Who did it?
hint.text: What was 'woven from recycled yarn and hand tufted'? A person, or the tapestries? Put that noun right after the comma.

hint.title: Verb count
hint.text: Cover the part between the dashes: 'Several advantages ____ acoustic waves as a promising alternative…'. Is there any main verb? If not, the blank has to be one.

hint.title: But/and/so test
hint.text: Sentence 1: the poem explores time and identity. Sentence 2: it also reflects on poetry and other art. A new point added on, or an example of the old one?

hint.title: Cover the middle
hint.text: Cover the part between the commas ('one of over 180…'). 'The African Games Co-production Market ____ the growth…'. One market = it or they?

hint.title: But/and/so test
hint.text: Sentence 1: the theory was an obvious next step. Sentence 2: so maybe it wasn't a coincidence two people found it. Swap in 'so'—does it fit?

hint.title: Pairs: match the mark
hint.text: Read further along: how does the aside 'or FESTAC '77, as the event was more commonly known' end? Match the mark on the other side.

b74f676f.label: timeline

hint.title: Timeline test
hint.text: The blank shares its subject with 'premiered' (Price premiered … and ____). Two verbs joined by 'and' should match in form and tense.

hint.title: Take-out test
hint.text: Take the names out: 'Paintings by the renowned US artists were featured…'. Which artists? Needed. Also: no comma between a subject and its verb ('were featured').

hint.title: Own-word test
hint.text: The text says they 'assumed' it, and the data later disproved it. Your own word: they ____ it (guessed). Then match.

hint.title: Point test
hint.text: Whose shores? Point at the owner: 'the North Sea' (one thing). Then the swap test: does 'on it is shores' make sense?

hint.title: Namely test
hint.text: Two jobs: 'though' is a little add-on word, so a comma sets it off. Then what follows explains 'more than just equations'. Which mark introduces an explanation?

hint.title: Cover the middle
hint.text: What helps it survive? Look right before 'that': 'coiled branching structures'. One thing or many?

hint.title: List test
hint.text: Look later in the list: 'research; and educating'. The first item is 'growing diverse plant species, both native and nonnative'. Match what separates the items.

hint.title: Cover the middle
hint.text: Cover 'of a ghazal's couplets' and the 'while…' part between commas. The subject starts with 'each one'. Is 'each one' it or they?

hint.title: Split test
hint.text: 'They are hardly pristine, though' is a full sentence. 'many chondrites experience aqueous alteration…' is another. 'though' belongs to the first one.

hint.title: Point test
hint.text: What consists of one or two suppliers? Point at it: 'a given industry' (one). The part between the dashes is extra—don't let 'water and electricity' fool you.

hint.title: Take-out test
hint.text: Take the name out: '…the work of little-known French portrait artist (1774–1821)'. Which artist? The name is needed, so nothing goes around it.

hint.title: Cover the middle
hint.text: The subject is 'her book's musings on tenth-century Japanese courtly life'. Cover 'on … life'. Musings = it or they?

hint.title: Namely test
hint.text: '…one trait that they scored particularly high on ____ openness to experience.' The end names the trait. Keep 'on' with 'high'. Which mark means 'namely'?

hint.title: Who did it?
hint.text: 'Compared with that of a highly concentrated market'—'that' means 'the score'. So a score is being compared. What must come right after the comma?

hint.title: Split test
hint.text: Where does sentence one really end? 'for one' is a little tag that belongs to the first example. Then 'The Katzenbach … decision … is another such event' stands alone.

hint.title: Goal checklist
hint.text: The goal has 2 parts: (1) the 1821 Declaration and (2) Valle's CHANGING beliefs (before and after). Cross out any choice that skips the declaration or doesn't show a change.

hint.title: Cover the middle
hint.text: Cover everything between the commas: 'Barrada's pieces ____ the ways humans…'. Swap in 'it' or 'they'—which one is it?

hint.title: Take-out test
hint.text: Remove 'however': 'Lai and Muñoz recognize the need for direct observation, recommending…'. One sentence or two? If it's one, 'however' just needs a matching pair.

hint.title: Point test
hint.text: Whose peers? Point at the owner: 'the Tajik Republic' (one). Then the swap test: does 'it is peer' make sense?

hint.title: Cover the middle
hint.text: Cover 'of these plays' and the 'which include…' part. The subject is 'each one'. It or they?

hint.title: Nothing: subject → verb
hint.text: Find the subject and its verb: 'her 2019 novel ____ offers…'. Would you ever put a mark between a subject and its own verb?

hint.title: Goal checklist
hint.text: Goal: Einstein's argument + its historical context (when, and what happened next). Does the choice state Einstein's view correctly AND place it in time? One choice flips Bohr's view.

hint.title: Verb count
hint.text: Main verb: 'begins'. Take out the words between the commas and the sentence still works. Can a describing add-on have its own main verb?

hint.title: But/and/so test
hint.text: Before: architects championed nature. After: the staircase couldn't really grow in a forest. More of the same, a result, or admitting something obvious?

hint.title: Namely test
hint.text: '…has detected exoplanets at vast distances from Earth' is a full sentence, and a list follows. Copy how the 2nd item is built: 'at 60 light-years away, the Neptune-like planet…'.

hint.title: Who did it?
hint.text: Who is 'forming extensive networks'? Not 'it', not 'transport', not 'nutrients'. Which living things form networks? They go right after the comma.

hint.title: Nothing: subject → verb
hint.text: 'The roughly 200,000 km² Puntland Desert' is one long subject and 'is classified' is its verb. Never put a mark inside a subject or between a subject and its verb.

hint.title: Cover the middle
hint.text: Cover 'of many fossilized microbacteria' and the 'which seem…' part. The subject is the noun before 'of': 'the presence'. It or they?

hint.title: Split test
hint.text: Does the first part end a complete thought at 'plant)'? The second part has its own subject and verb ('she found'). Who is doing the 'researching'?

hint.title: Own-word test
hint.text: Cover the choices. Three years, 250,000 images, 'painstakingly', inventing new tools… Say your own word: 'it was a very ____ process.' Then match it.

hint.title: Split test
hint.text: Both sides are full sentences ('Saville is not the protagonist…' / 'she's the occasion of it'). A comma alone can't join them, even with a word like 'rather'.

hint.title: Split test
hint.text: Both halves have their own subject + verb ('The city … partnered' / 'the AI algorithm determines'). The 'analyzing' piece belongs to the second half. What can separate two sentences?

hint.title: List test
hint.text: The list: spiral lines…, depictions of animals…, and enamel accents. Look at the mark right before 'and inlaid enamel accents'. Match it.

hint.title: Take-out test
hint.text: Take the name out: 'of keen interest to linguist of the University of Toronto.' Which linguist? Needed → no commas.

hint.title: Take-out test
hint.text: Take the name out: 'chemistry professor and his colleagues…'. Which professor? You can't tell, so the name is needed. Needed info gets no commas.

hint.title: Split test
hint.text: 'these elected officials take turns…' is a full sentence. Is 'does not have one president but three' a full sentence too? A who-clause can't glue two sentences together.
